content: Palliative care is essential across all medical fields that involve the treatment of patients with severe or life-threatening illnesses. This includes, but is not limited to, pediatrics, oncology, infectious diseases, geriatrics, internal medicine, hematology, critical care, family medicine, tuberculosis, hepatology, neurology, cardiology, pulmonology, nephrology, neonatology, traumatology, anesthesiology, and surgery. Training in these areas should encompass both theoretical classroom instruction and practical, supervised clinical experiences. Specialists in these fields, particularly those working in hospitals, must be equipped to provide direct palliative care to their patients. Physicians who are part of hospital-based palliative care teams, whether full-time or part-time, should have at least intermediate-level training in palliative care. Ideally, interdisciplinary palliative care teams (IDTs) in secondary and tertiary hospitals should be led by physicians who are specialists in palliative care. To achieve this, lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) should prioritize the development of palliative care specialist training programs to ensure an adequate supply of trained physicians for their regions. These training programs should last at least one year, though the duration may vary depending on the postgraduate medical training regulations of each country. While it is preferable for clinicians providing pediatric palliative care (PPC) to be fully trained in pediatrics and exclusively care for children, generalist clinicians such as general practitioners, family doctors, and primary care nurses should also be trained and competent to provide PPC when pediatric specialists are unavailable or unnecessary. Basic and intermediate-level palliative care training focuses on essential competencies rather than specialization. These competencies include understanding the principles of palliative care, effective communication, optimizing comfort and quality of life, care planning and collaborative practice, addressing loss, grief, and bereavement, maintaining professional and ethical standards, and fostering professional resilience. Generalists providing PPC should have access to advice from a pediatrician with intermediate-level palliative care training or a palliative care specialist physician at any time, particularly in rural areas where task-shifting and task-sharing are critical. Essential competencies in PPC include age-appropriate symptom assessment (e.g., pain, nausea, dyspnea, anxiety, depression), appropriate medication selection and administration based on pediatric pharmacokinetics, and the use of both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic therapies. Emergency plans should be developed, and caregivers should be trained to manage medications at home. Psychosocial assessment and intervention are also vital, addressing the child’s and family’s understanding of the illness, fears, coping mechanisms, and communication styles. Care plans should be adjusted accordingly, and tools like play therapy, music, and art can be used to support emotional expression and distraction. Recognizing the unique disease trajectories in children compared to adults is crucial. Anticipatory guidance should be provided to reduce fear of the unknown, and communication should be developmentally appropriate. Children should be included in decision-making processes as appropriate for their developmental stage, and care plans should respect cultural norms, ethical principles, and legal guidelines. Spiritual concerns should also be addressed, with referrals to spiritual care providers when necessary. The goals of care should be clearly defined, whether they focus on cure, maintenance of health, comfort, or a combination of these. When intensive life-sustaining treatments are not aligned with the goals of care, appropriate orders should be written to protect the patient from unnecessary interventions. Care plans should integrate the patient’s symptoms, disease trajectory, and the desires and goals of the patient and family. Guidance should be provided on the best location for care (e.g., home, hospital, hospice) to achieve these goals, and tangible needs such as medical equipment, social supports, and community services should be addressed. Access to essential medicines, particularly strong opioids like morphine, is critical for managing pain in conditions such as cancer, HIV/AIDS, and other serious illnesses. Despite being included on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, morphine is often inaccessible in adequate amounts and appropriate forms in many parts of the world. Approximately 75% of the global population lacks access to morphine or other strong opioids when clinically indicated for pain management. Barriers to opioid availability include overly restrictive regulations, inadequate education of healthcare providers on pain management, and a lack of understanding among drug regulators about the appropriate use of opioids. Governments must ensure that all physicians involved in patient care are legally and institutionally authorized to prescribe and administer strong opioids like morphine based on medical need. They must also ensure a sufficient supply of morphine to meet all medical needs. While the misuse of controlled substances poses societal risks, regulatory systems should not create barriers to the legitimate medical use of opioids. Efforts should be made to identify and address barriers to opioid availability, such as restrictive prescribing regulations, limited education of healthcare providers, and supply chain failures. Health systems should establish mechanisms to monitor the flow of opioids from import or manufacture to patient use. These systems should ensure continued availability of opioids for medical purposes without interfering with access. Stock-outs and supply chain failures can lead to patient suffering, withdrawal symptoms, and increased risks of illicit opioid use and suicide. Countries are required to report annual opioid consumption to the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB), which uses this data to estimate global opioid needs and allocate appropriate quantities. Increases in allocations can be requested based on improved healthcare services or revised disease prevalence estimates. Integrating palliative care and symptom relief into healthcare systems can strengthen these systems and promote universal health coverage (UHC). Palliative care has been associated with improved patient outcomes, including better symptom control, reduced spiritual distress, enhanced quality of life, and increased patient and family satisfaction. It also reduces healthcare costs by decreasing the number of physician visits, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and intensive care unit stays at the end of life.
